problem: Visual navigation and embodied QA benchmarks (R2R, IQA/IQUAD V1, EQA) were published with only random, heuristic or majority-class baselines. Those baselines cannot show how much of a multimodal model's performance comes from unimodal dataset biases (language-only, vision-only, or action-history-only regularities) rather than grounded vision-language reasoning.
motivation: All datasets have biases. A baseline should capture them, so that beating it means the task is actually being solved. NLP work (hypothesis-only NLI) and VQA work (answering without the image) showed that deep models exploit such shortcuts. The authors observe that in egocentric navigation even the action history and the 'minimally sensed' set of available actions carry strong signal: peaked action-transition distributions let an agent memorize simple rules.
key_idea: Re-train each benchmark's published model with one or more input modalities (vision, language) replaced by zero vectors, keeping architecture and parameter count fixed. Use the resulting action-only, vision+action and language+action ablations as the baselines multimodal methods must beat.
insight: Unimodal ablations beat every published baseline and sometimes beat the full multimodal model. On R2R with teacher forcing, the language+action ablation reaches 22.1% SR on val-unseen versus 19.6% for the full Seq2Seq model. On EQA navigation, vision+action ties with or beats the full model in all but one setting, suggesting the EQA navigator ignores the question. On EQA QA, a language-only model gets 48.8% versus the 19.8% majority baseline, because each question has one dominant answer. Even an action-history-only agent with just the available-action mask W beats the random/heuristic baselines, by exploiting topological trajectory biases. The teacher- vs student-forcing ablation shows the effect depends on training regime: with student forcing (more exploration) the full R2R model reaches 21.8% SR on val-unseen, far above all unimodal ablations (best 13.9%). This suggests student forcing is what lets the model actually align vision and language.
method: Ablation framework: a_t = M(V_t, L, A_{t-1}; W) using each paper's released code and training paradigm; ablations zero out inputs (A = action only, A+V = vision+action, A+L = language+action), preserving architecture and parameter count.

R2R: Anderson et al. Seq2Seq model (LSTM language encoder; LSTM decoder with ResNet image features and previous action; attention over instruction). Ablations trained with teacher forcing (main table) and with student forcing (best validation SR across epochs).

THOR-Nav (new benchmark from a subset of IQUAD V1 questions): agent starts at a random spot and must approach a fridge, garbage can or microwave given a question. Uses Gordon et al.'s CNN over image + GT semantic segmentation + tiled question + previous action, trained with teacher forcing.

EQA navigation: Das et al. hierarchical planner-controller LSTM (PACMAN-style) with CNN image features, LSTM question encoding and previous action. Evaluated by final distance to target (d_T) and minimum distance along the path (d_min) from 10/30/50 actions away, on the authors' expanded EQA data.

QA decoupled from navigation: IQA QA uses GT top-down object locations tiled with the question (convs + spatial sum + FC). EQA QA uses the ShortestPath+VQA model with attention over the last 5 gold-path frames. Only V-only and L-only ablations here, since QA models take no action input.

setting.backbone: Published task models retrained with zeroed inputs: Anderson et al. Seq2Seq (LSTM enc-dec + ResNet features) for R2R; Gordon et al. IQA CNN navigator/QA net; Das et al. EQA planner-controller LSTM + CNN and ShortestPath+VQA
setting.training_data: Each benchmark's own training set only (R2R train; IQUAD V1 / THOR-Nav subset; EQA v1 expanded data released by the authors); no extra data
setting.observation: R2R: egocentric RGB (ResNet features); THOR-Nav: egocentric RGB + GT semantic segmentation; EQA: egocentric RGB (CNN); plus previous action and available-action mask W
setting.action_space: R2R: low-level Forward / turn Left & Right / tilt Up & Down / End on the nav graph; THOR: discrete steps of 0.25 m and turns; EQA: discrete forward/turn/stop via planner + controller; QA: answer classification
setting.privileged: Available-action mask W for all navigators; GT semantic segmentation for THOR-Nav; GT top-down object locations for IQA QA (replaces exploration); gold shortest-path frames for EQA QA; R2R student-forcing results use best validation epoch

numbers_note: This is an analysis paper, so the 'own method' rows are unimodal ablations of published models. Full-model and baseline rows (e.g., R2R full Seq2Seq 27.1/19.6 teacher forcing and 38.6/21.8 student forcing; EQA full 4.17 m; EQA QA full 64.0) are baselines and are excluded. R2R is evaluated on validation. The student-forcing table reports the highest validation SR across epochs. For THOR-Nav, IQUAD and EQA the paper only labels columns Seen/Unseen, so the split names chosen here are best guesses. EQA numbers use the authors' expanded data and do not match Das et al. IQA QA uses GT full-scene views and is not comparable to Gordon et al. No SPL or other R2R metrics are reported. Figures (action distributions, qualitative EQA) contain no additional numbers.
results: Unimodal ablations beat every published baseline, by up to 29% absolute (EQA QA: language-only 48.8 vs majority 19.8). On THOR-Nav, vision+action reaches 35.6% SR (seen) vs 2.18% for the random baseline. In unseen environments they can also beat the full model. On R2R val-unseen with teacher forcing, language+action gets 22.1% SR vs the full Seq2Seq's 19.6%. On EQA navigation (30 actions away), vision+action gets 4.11 m vs the full model's 4.17 m. Under student forcing, however, the full R2R model (21.8% unseen) clearly beats all unimodal ablations (best 13.9%).
limitations: Only one published model per benchmark is ablated; ablation is done by zeroing inputs within that fixed architecture, not with purpose-built unimodal models, and results come from single runs without variance.

QA is evaluated with privileged ground-truth views or gold navigation, and EQA uses expanded data, so QA and EQA numbers are not directly comparable to the original papers; exact eval splits are not always stated.

The strength of the unimodal effect depends on the training regime: with student forcing the R2R full model dominates, so the teacher-forcing conclusions do not transfer to stronger training setups; only success rate / distance metrics are reported.
